review.title: Tissue sampling after inadequate neck FNA

cues.phrase: A third identical fine-needle aspiration
cues.why: 'Third identical' openly labels the option as repetition of an already unsuccessful procedure rather than a credible optimized sampling plan.

cues.phrase: could not classify the process or complete the required ancillary studies
cues.why: This legitimate specimen limitation points to greater tissue acquisition; paired with an explicitly identical repeat and an open incision, it makes the core option the conspicuous intermediate choice.

fairness: Image-guided core biopsy is defensible to obtain additional tissue after these FNAs, and recognizing the material limitation before changing technique can be meaningful two-step reasoning.

The appropriate architecture-preserving sampling route depends on suspected lymphoid disease, node accessibility, pathology needs and local expertise. Excisional biopsy may be a credible competitor; it should not be silently represented by the less well-defined 'open incisional biopsy'.
The broad task 'consider' can encompass more than one reasonable approach. The supplied facts do not prove that core is uniquely preferable in every suspected lymphoid process.

Importance: high practical value in neck-node diagnosis and tissue stewardship. Realism: solid-target documentation is useful, but the repeat sampling strategy should be tied to the pathologist's concrete material requirements.
suggestions: State the actual missing tissue/ancillary requirement and node accessibility, then ask for the preferred next approach under those conditions.
Compare core with a genuine optimized FNA or excisional-biopsy strategy; remove 'third identical' and have a clinician adjudicate the closest surgical-biopsy alternative.

review.title: Tissue sampling after inadequate neck FNA

cues.phrase: Contrast CT shows a percutaneous route to its solid portion
cues.why: Gives feasibility permission matching image-guided core biopsy.

cues.phrase: surgical removal would require dissection beside the carotid sheath
cues.why: Preloads the reason to avoid excision and is repeated in the excision option.

cues.phrase: the least invasive next sampling approach
cues.why: With FNA already repeated and intact architecture requested, the lead-in tells the reader to choose the middle invasiveness option rather than compare diagnostic adequacy.

cues.phrase: the pathologist requests intact tissue relationships
cues.why: Supplies the tissue-requirement interpretation, leaving a familiar FNA-versus-core-versus-excision ladder.

fairness: Image-guided core biopsy is plausible for an accessible deep node when further architecture is needed. Open excision can also be justified for some suspected lymphoid processes; the requested degree of architecture and local pathology expectations would affect adequacy.

Importance: useful tissue-acquisition judgment within general surgery. Realism: deep-node procedural risk is real, but the paired access/risk sentences and least-invasive task are heavily engineered to select core. Too easy as written; do not claim core is universally sufficient for lymphoma classification.
suggestions: Ask a neutral next-biopsy decision with a specific unresolved diagnostic requirement and comparable realistic acquisition plans.

Retain true anatomical risk and access observations, but remove rationale-like feasibility permission and the leading 'least invasive' instruction unless invasiveness itself is the explicitly accepted basic objective.

review.title: Tissue sampling after inadequate neck FNA

cues.phrase: Two ultrasound-guided FNAs
cues.why: The repeated failed sampling route makes a third FNA an obvious reuse foil unless its on-site preparation would address a clearly specified prior deficiency.

cues.phrase: behind the internal jugular vein and against the carotid sheath
cues.why: Acts as a risk cue against open excision without establishing that a core needle has a safer feasible path; this can bias the key without resolving safety.

fairness: Recognizing a classification/architecture problem and choosing a tissue route is meaningful. However, suspected lymphoid disease may require architecture and sufficient tissue for full classification; core and excision can both be defensible depending on feasibility and diagnostic requirements. CT depth alone does not establish core as the unique best route.

Importance: useful general-surgery neck-node workup. Realism: an enlarging deep node after two nondiagnostic classifications is plausible, but acquisition safety and pathologist material requirements are decision-critical omissions.
suggestions: Specify whether architecture, additional ancillary material, or both are required, and provide actual imaging evidence of feasible needle and surgical routes.
Compare acquisitions capable of meeting the requirement. Do not imply proximity to vessels is by itself proof that percutaneous core is safer than excision.

review.title: Sampling a recurrent cystic neck mass

cues.phrase: tissue projecting into the cavity from its wall
cues.why: Paired with 'core biopsy of mural tissue', this nearly names the target. The shortcut is partial because 'mural' requires vocabulary knowledge. The raw target description is appropriate; the problem is that no other option offers a credible targeted needle assessment.

cues.phrase: The first needle pass entered its fluid-containing centre; the specimen contains macrophages and proteinaceous material without lesional epithelial or lymphoid cells.
cues.why: Together with refilling, this explicitly contrasts the failed fluid sample with the newly described wall tissue. A reader can follow a general 'sample the other part' repair narrative without much neck-mass reasoning. It is useful adequacy evidence, but weak alternatives make the correction too transparent.

fairness: Original flag fully resolved: yes for neck-versus-cervix wording. The mass is explicitly lateral neck. General-surgery scope is a recorded owner/manager decision, not a new claim of independently verified ABSITE coverage.

Further representative needle sampling is the best offered approach; open excision and surveillance are not comparably strong next choices in the supplied scenario. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in using a targeted core as an offered plan.

The supplied observations do not establish that core biopsy is uniquely preferable to a repeat targeted FNA, which is not offered. Omitting that close competitor makes this easier; it is not by itself proof of two correct answers among the current options.

Two steps are present: recognize that cyst-fluid sampling did not adequately sample the lesion, then choose a representative target/technique. This is likely easy for PGY-2/3 given the current alternatives. The prose image description supports the decision, but no actual image exhibit is supplied.
suggestions: Compare credible repeat needle strategies with concrete target and technique labels; include the closest clinically defensible alternative only after the clinician/source review can distinguish it from the key.

Do not claim that one fluid-only pass universally mandates core biopsy. Supply the verified adequacy, sampling or diagnostic requirement that actually determines technique, or test target selection without overclaiming technique superiority.

Keep 'neck' and the raw specimen observations. If an imaging interpretation objective is retained, a reviewed constructed exhibit could carry the localization information without a sentence that effectively names the next target.

question.stem: Which diagnostic role describes this patient's completed contrast-enhanced neck CT?

answerChoices.label: Microscopic cellular classification
answerChoices.distractorRationale: That role requires assessment of sampled cells or tissue, which the supplied CT did not obtain.

answerChoices.label: Definitive tissue diagnosis
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The supplied CT characterizes anatomy; the undiagnosed mass still requires appropriate tissue assessment.

answerChoices.label: Histological tumor grading
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The supplied CT did not obtain a histological specimen.

question.explanation: The correct answer is “Anatomical characterization.” Contrast-enhanced neck CT helps describe the mass and cervical anatomy. It does not replace the appropriate needle sample needed to establish a tissue diagnosis.

answerChoices.label: Repeat empiric antibacterial therapy

question.stem: Which diagnostic request should be made next for {patientName}'s neck mass?

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of mural tissue
answerChoices.rationale: The fluid-only result does not establish the nature of the mural tissue. Directing the needle into that component corrects the specific representativeness problem without treating the fluid as a benign diagnosis.

answerChoices.label: Open excisional biopsy of the entire neck mass
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An intact specimen is tempting after a failed sample, but a representative needle approach remains available before an open diagnostic operation in this at-risk adult neck mass.

answerChoices.label: Interval ultrasound surveillance of the neck mass
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Surveillance treats the cyst-fluid result as sufficient reassurance, although it does not represent the vascular mural component in this persistent adult neck mass.

question.explanation: A macrophage-rich aspirate from the fluid centre is not a representative diagnosis of the mural component. Request image-guided tissue sampling directed at that component; core biopsy can provide tissue after the inadequate fluid aspirate. Representative targeted FNA can also be appropriate, and the question does not rank it as an incorrect alternative. The fluid result does not establish a basis for surveillance, and an open diagnostic operation need not precede a representative needle approach.
question.teachingPoint: A macrophage-rich aspirate from the fluid centre is not a representative diagnosis of the mural component. question.stem: Which initial tissue-sampling referral is most appropriate for {patientName}'s assessed lateral neck lymph node?

answerChoices.label: Open incisional biopsy of the neck node
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An open incision is not the preferred initial sample among these offered approaches before needle assessment.

answerChoices.label: Open excisional biopsy of the neck node

question.explanation: For this assessed, undiagnosed adult neck lymph node, FNA is the appropriate offered initial needle approach rather than starting with open biopsy. proposedNodes.objective: Distinguish missing transferred images from an unperformed neck examination
proposedNodes.task: Which imaging action should be requested next for {patientName}'s persistent neck mass?

choices.label: Retrieve the prior contrast-enhanced neck CT series
choices.rationale: The acquisition record documents a completed contrast examination with the relevant deep coverage; the local export is incomplete. Obtain that examination for review before duplicating it.
choices.temptation: Resolve the missing anatomical information using the examination already acquired.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If the contrast series had never been acquired, retrieval could not supply the missing information.

choices.label: Acquire a new contrast-enhanced neck CT examination
choices.rationale: A new CT could answer the question, but the documented completed study should first be obtained and assessed while the clinical findings are unchanged.
choices.temptation: The ultrasound did not show the lower margin, and the local images do not show contrast enhancement.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: A prior examination without the required acquisition, inadequate images, or a new clinical change could justify a new CT.

choices.label: Acquire a new Doppler ultrasound neck examination
choices.rationale: Doppler may help characterize accessible tissue and vessels, but does not replace the documented cross-sectional examination for the retroclavicular extent.
choices.temptation: The mass can be found by ultrasound without another CT exposure.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: A different unresolved superficial vascular or targeting question could warrant Doppler ultrasound.

proposedNodes.explanation: The absent contrast images in the clinic export are not evidence that contrast imaging was never performed. The outside acquisition log and report describe a completed neck study covering the deep margin. Retrieve and review that study first; repeat imaging remains appropriate if it proves inadequate or the clinical question changes.
steps: Distinguish an incomplete transferred image set from an incomplete original acquisition.
Use the documented adequate prior acquisition to seek its images before ordering a duplicate examination.

proposedNodes.decider: The original acquisition log documents contrast neck images through the retroclavicular margin, whereas the transferred file contains only localizer and unenhanced images.
proposedNodes.consequence: Duplicate exposure and another examination without first using the relevant existing study.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: If the outside log showed that the contrast acquisition was cancelled, a new dedicated contrast neck CT would be the best offered action.
proposedNodes.attack: All three labels are neutral imaging actions of similar specificity. No body-staging foil or assertion that MRI is inferior remains. Repetition is genuinely plausible from the incomplete local file; the original acquisition record, rather than a repeat label, decides whether a second acquisition is needed.

proposedNodes.deletion: Remove the original acquisition log and the distinction between a missing export and an unperformed examination becomes unresolved. proposedNodes.objective: Identify an unrepresented index neck lesion before choosing its initial sample
proposedNodes.task: Which sampling procedure should be requested for {patientName}'s dominant cervical mass?

choices.label: Ultrasound-guided FNA of the enhancing nodule in lesion B
choices.rationale: The benign report belongs to A. B remains unrepresented, and its accessible enhancing nodule is an appropriate initial image-guided target.
choices.temptation: Tie the pathological result to the index lesion before applying an acquisition sequence.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If the specimen record instead showed an adequate representative sample from B, the next step would depend on that result and its concordance.

choices.label: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the solid node labelled A
choices.rationale: More tissue from A would not establish the diagnosis of the unsampled dominant mass B. This is a target error, not a claim that core biopsy is generally inferior.
choices.temptation: A core offers more tissue when an initial needle report appears discordant with the concerning neck finding.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If A were the index suspicious lesion and its representative FNA were inadequate for the required assessment, a core could be appropriate.

choices.label: Open excisional biopsy of the dominant mass labelled B
choices.rationale: The concerning lesion is accessible for initial needle sampling. The report from a different node does not establish failure of an appropriate needle evaluation of B.
choices.temptation: Excision would provide substantial material from the lesion that matters.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Open acquisition may be needed after an appropriate specialist workup when a required diagnosis cannot be obtained by the relevant needle route.

proposedNodes.currentUpdate: Review of the contrast CT identifies the dominant partly fluid-containing mass as lesion B. An enhancing nodule along its wall is accessible by ultrasound; the thyroid and salivary glands are separate and there is no continuity with a major vessel. A smaller solid node just above it is labelled A. An outside FNA report describes benign lymphocytes, but its saved needle image and specimen worksheet identify node A. Lesion B has not been sampled.
proposedNodes.explanation: Match a specimen to the lesion it actually sampled. Benign lymphocytes from A do not explain B. For the unsampled partly cystic index lesion, obtain an image-guided FNA directed at its enhancing nodule before treating a sample from another node as a failed workup of B. Core biopsy is not rejected as a technique; the offered core targets the other node.
steps: Use the needle image and worksheet to recognize that the benign result belongs to another node.
Select a representative initial needle target in the unsampled index lesion rather than escalate sampling of the wrong node or proceed to open biopsy.
proposedNodes.closestError: Treat the benign FNA as a discordant sample of B and obtain a core from the previously sampled node.
proposedNodes.decider: The needle image and worksheet identify A, while the dominant enhancing-wall lesion is B.
proposedNodes.consequence: A technically successful additional sample may still leave the index neck lesion undiagnosed.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: If the image and worksheet identified B as adequately sampled and pathology required additional architecture, the current initial-target rationale would no longer determine the next procedure.
proposedNodes.attack: The lead-in uses sampling rather than tissue and every option names technique plus target. The core option is credible as an escalation for apparent discordance, but is distinguished by the documented target identity. No claim ranks core below FNA for all cystic neck masses; no fluid-versus-tissue word match alone decides the item.

proposedNodes.objective: Choose architectural tissue despite a plausible improved needle target
proposedNodes.task: Which biopsy should be requested next to classify {patientName}'s cervical lymphoid process?

choices.label: Excisional biopsy of the accessible superficial node
choices.rationale: The suspected T-cell lymphoid process still needs intact nodal organization for classification. The clinically accessible node offers surgical architectural assessment.
choices.temptation: Obtain the type of material required rather than only increase the number of atypical cells.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If surgical acquisition were not feasible, multiple carefully targeted cores could be the practical alternative.

choices.label: Core biopsies of viable peripheral tissue in the larger node
choices.rationale: Changing from the necrotic center to viable peripheral tissue could improve yield, but does not provide the intact organization sought when surgical tissue is feasible for this T-cell differential.
choices.temptation: The first cores predominantly sampled necrosis, making better targeting a real opportunity.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If surgery were not possible, a planned set of viable cores for histology and ancillary studies could be used with its diagnostic limitations.

choices.label: FNA of the superficial node with cell block and flow cytometry
choices.rationale: Ancillary cytology may characterize cells, but does not supply the nodal organization missing from the classification workup.
choices.temptation: An accessible different node and planned ancillary studies could produce a better cytological specimen.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: FNA and flow can be useful for selected questions about an already classified lymphoid process rather than initial architectural classification.

proposedNodes.explanation: Cell detection and lymphoma classification are different endpoints. Better targeting could recover more viable cells from the larger node, but the suspected T-cell process still requires assessment of nodal organization. Surgical sampling is preferred when feasible; the superficial accessible node makes excision the best offered way to obtain that material. Needle approaches remain alternatives when surgical sampling is not feasible.
steps: Distinguish poor yield from the larger node from the separate unresolved need for nodal organization in a suspected T-cell process.
Choose intact surgical tissue from the accessible node rather than improve cell yield alone.

proposedNodes.decider: Hematopathology still cannot classify the T-cell process without nodal organization, and a superficial mobile node is clinically accessible.
proposedNodes.consequence: Another sample may recover viable atypical cells yet still fail to establish the required classification.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: If surgical sampling were not feasible, the optimized viable peripheral core plan would become the best offered acquisition despite its limitations.

proposedNodes.objective: Choose intervention for a fixed accessible duct stone
proposedNodes.task: Which intervention should be recommended next for {patientName}'s submandibular duct stone?

choices.label: Transoral duct incision and stone extraction
choices.rationale: The reachable fixed distal stone allows a duct approach that preserves the gland.
choices.temptation: Use actual site and retrieval limitations rather than jump to gland removal.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: An inaccessible intraparenchymal stone would require a different plan.

choices.label: Extracorporeal shock-wave stone fragmentation
choices.rationale: This serves selected stones not directly accessible through a duct approach.
choices.temptation: A failed basket can make lithotripsy seem the automatic next step.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: A symptomatic poorly accessible intraparenchymal stone may justify specialist lithotripsy.

choices.label: Transcervical submandibular gland excision
choices.rationale: Gland removal is disproportionate before addressing this accessible duct stone.
choices.temptation: Recurrent symptoms may be mistaken for irreversible gland failure.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Persistent symptomatic disease after suitable alternatives can warrant gland excision.

choices.label: Clinical follow-up for recurrent gland symptoms

choices.temptation: An inaccessible residual focus can seem to demand definitive clearance.

choices.label: Ultrasound-guided core needle sampling for histology

choices.temptation: A histological specimen may resolve an indeterminate epithelial-neoplasm assessment.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: A clinician-supported diagnostic requirement that this cytology cannot satisfy could establish a stronger case-specific ranking.

choices.label: Ultrasound-guided FNA with on-site assessment and cell block

choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: This could be selected when optimized cytology can answer the documented unresolved diagnostic question.

choices.label: Open incisional sampling of the parotid lesion

proposedNodes.task: Which imaging request should be made next for {patientName}'s new facial findings?

choices.label: Acquire contrast MRI of the facial nerve course through the skull base
choices.rationale: The motor pattern involves upper and lower facial branches. With parotid carcinoma, assess the facial nerve course for spread; the relevant proximal course was not acquired in the earlier gland study.
choices.temptation: Combine motor localization with the actual boundaries of the previous examination.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If the complete relevant course had already been adequately acquired for these findings, review or reformats of that study might avoid another acquisition.

choices.label: Reformat the prior parotid MRI along the facial nerve course
choices.rationale: Reformats cannot show anatomy outside the original acquisition. A complete transferred study is still incomplete for this new nerve-course question.
choices.temptation: The prior study used contrast and has already characterized the gland; reuse could avoid another scan.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If the relevant proximal nerve course were contained in an adequate original acquisition, targeted review or reformats could answer the question.

choices.label: Acquire contrast MRI of the trigeminal nerve course through the skull base
choices.rationale: The raw deficit is facial movement across upper and lower branches, with preserved facial sensation. A trigeminal-course study does not target the implicated motor pathway.
choices.temptation: Salivary cancers can spread along sensory as well as motor cranial nerves.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: New altered sensation in a defined trigeminal distribution would shift targeted nerve-course assessment toward that pathway.

proposedNodes.currentUpdate: At the current clinic examination, right forehead wrinkling, forceful eye closure and the smile are all weaker than at the earlier visit. Facial sensation to light touch is symmetric. The prior MRI acquisition record confirms that imaging ended below the temporal bone; those more proximal structures were not scanned.
proposedNodes.explanation: Weak forehead movement, eye closure and smile localize the deficit to the facial motor pathway rather than a facial sensory pathway. In parotid carcinoma this raises concern for neural spread without proving it. Request a focused contrast MRI covering the facial nerve through the skull base. The earlier gland acquisition cannot be reconstructed to show proximal anatomy it never included.
steps: Localize the new upper- and lower-face motor deficit to the facial nerve rather than a trigeminal sensory distribution.
Use the recorded acquisition boundary to request new relevant nerve-course coverage instead of reformats of anatomy never scanned.

proposedNodes.decider: Weak forehead, eye closure and smile identify the motor pathway, and the original acquisition ends below its proximal temporal-bone course.
proposedNodes.consequence: An apparently reassuring review could leave the clinically implicated nerve course unexamined.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: If the prior MRI contained adequate full-course facial-nerve coverage for the current findings, targeted review or reformats could replace a new acquisition; trigeminal sensory loss would instead change the nerve targeted.

proposedNodes.objective: Select immediate facial-nerve reconstruction from stump availability and repair tension
proposedNodes.task: During {patientName}'s recorded parotid operation, which immediate facial-nerve reconstruction best fits these findings?

choices.label: Interposition cable graft between the facial nerve stumps
choices.rationale: The identified viable proximal and distal facial stumps permit facial-to-facial reconstruction, but a graft is needed to bridge a repair that otherwise requires sustained traction.
choices.temptation: Restore continuity using the available facial nerve while avoiding tension.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If the stumps met without tension, direct repair could avoid an interposition graft.

choices.label: Direct end-to-end repair between the facial nerve stumps
choices.rationale: Direct repair is attractive with both stumps present, but the described sustained traction does not meet the requirement for a tension-free repair.
choices.temptation: Immediate direct coaptation avoids graft harvest and an additional junction.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If mobilization allowed the viable stumps to meet without tension, direct microsurgical repair would be appropriate.

choices.label: Hypoglossal-to-facial nerve anastomosis to the distal stump
choices.rationale: A viable proximal facial stump is available for reconstruction. A donor-nerve plan does not resolve the case as well as bridging the gap between the available facial stumps.
choices.temptation: Donor-nerve reanimation can restore input to distal facial branches.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If no usable proximal facial stump were available, donor-nerve reanimation could be considered.

proposedNodes.explanation: This is a documented nerve discontinuity, so observation for transient weakness does not restore its continuity. Both viable facial stumps are available, but direct approximation requires sustained traction. An interposition cable graft preserves a facial-to-facial reconstruction without a tense direct repair. A donor-nerve strategy is considered when a suitable proximal facial stump is unavailable; the exact reconstruction needs specialist judgment.
steps: Recognize an actual divided nerve with usable proximal and distal facial stumps, rather than a continuity-preserved transient deficit.
Use the failure of tension-free approximation to choose a facial-to-facial graft over direct repair or a substitute donor nerve.
proposedNodes.closestError: Choose direct repair solely because both facial stumps are identified.
proposedNodes.decider: After mobilization, the viable stumps meet only under sustained traction; the proximal facial stump remains usable.
proposedNodes.consequence: A tense direct repair is selected despite the opportunity to bridge the defect, or an available proximal facial input is bypassed unnecessarily.
proposedNodes.counterfactual: If the mobilized stumps met without tension, direct repair would become the best offered reconstruction; if the proximal facial stump were unusable, a donor-nerve strategy would need consideration.
proposedNodes.attack: Every answer is an immediate reconstruction plan with comparable specificity. The original functioning and separable-nerve observations remain in the record; a separately documented iatrogenic division creates the new repair tradeoff. No gross invasion is introduced, and no internal withheld-language appears in the clinical explanation.

proposedNodes.task: Which postoperative plan should {patientName}'s clinic recommend for discussion with the head-and-neck team?

choices.label: Postoperative radiotherapy to the operative region
choices.rationale: Tumor growth inside small nerve sheaths is an adverse feature despite clear margins.
choices.temptation: Do not let favorable grade and margins erase neural involvement.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: A small completely resected low-grade tumor without adverse features could be followed.

choices.label: MRI surveillance of the operative region
choices.rationale: Size, grade and margin status do not negate the new perineural adverse feature.
choices.temptation: The small low-grade tumor is completely removed.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: The same favorable tumor without perineural or other adverse findings could support surveillance.

choices.label: Postoperative cisplatin with regional radiotherapy
choices.rationale: Routine chemotherapy addition has no established benefit in this setting.
choices.temptation: A resident may import concurrent chemoradiation rules from mucosal squamous cancers.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: A separately supported disease-specific indication or a clinical trial would require different evidence.

proposedNodes.currentUpdate: Final pathology shows the small low-grade tumor completely excised with uninvolved inked margins. In sections away from the main facial nerve, tumor nests are present inside the sheaths of small nerves. Regional nodes are negative.
proposedNodes.explanation: Tumor within small nerve sheaths is perineural growth. It supports postoperative local radiotherapy discussion despite clear resection; it does not prove that the spared main facial nerve should have been removed. Routine cisplatin addition is unsupported.

proposedNodes.counterfactual: Remove the small-nerve involvement and retain a small low-grade completely excised tumor without other adverse features; surveillance becomes defensible.

proposedNodes.task: Which CT protocol should be requested at that point in {patientName}'s outside admission?

choices.label: Neck and chest CT with intravenous contrast in the venous phase
choices.rationale: The mismatch between improving neck swelling and persistent fever with new retrosternal pain raises concern for extension beyond the drained neck compartment. Venous-phase contrast soft-tissue imaging maps that extent.
choices.temptation: Match both the coverage and contrast phase to a possible connected soft-tissue complication.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: If the clinical question were an acute arterial lesion rather than soft-tissue infection, an arterial protocol would be selected instead.

choices.label: Neck and chest CT angiography with arterial-phase contrast
choices.rationale: Arterial angiography targets an arterial question. The described postoperative infectious course calls for venous-phase assessment of soft tissues and collections, not a primary arterial study.
choices.temptation: New chest pain can prompt a search for a vascular cause and an angiographic examination covers both regions.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Abrupt pain with findings suggesting an acute arterial lesion would support an arterial angiographic protocol.

choices.label: Neck and chest CT without intravenous contrast administration
choices.rationale: Unenhanced CT may show gas and gross extent but lacks the contrast assessment of soft-tissue enhancement needed for this complicated infection question.
choices.temptation: The dental source, potential gas and recent procedure make an anatomic survey seem sufficient.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: An urgent gas or bone question with a genuine contraindication to contrast could alter the protocol; that is a different tradeoff.

proposedNodes.explanation: Improving external neck swelling does not establish control of a deep infection when fever persists and retrosternal pain appears. Reassess the connected neck and chest soft tissues with intravenous contrast CT timed for venous-phase evaluation. An arterial angiogram addresses a different primary question, while unenhanced CT does not adequately characterize the enhancing soft tissues and possible collections.

choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Documented thoracic extent and anatomy inaccessible to adequate cervical drainage could favor thoracic access after specialist assessment.

Symptoms and examination have not changed since that CT. She has no fever, tenderness or airway symptoms.

review.title: R01 — Imaging an incompletely visualized persistent neck mass
fairness: Contrast-enhanced neck CT is the defensible best offered study for this incompletely mapped persistent adult neck lesion. MRI is not offered, so its potential appropriateness does not create a second key.
The task is complete and the presentation supplies age, sex, clinical stability and the relevant ultrasound limitation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The imaging task already presupposes further assessment. Persistence does not supply a separate consequential inference within these options: repeat the limited study, obtain local cross-sectional imaging, or undertake systemic metabolic imaging. This is a familiar modality-selection rule with weak competition, rather than two consequential steps.
R01's explanation does not disclose R02's sampling technique or target. The transition from ultrasound to the subsequent CT record is coherent.

Review-wide scope: all 12 proposed executable nodes were assessed using their candidate presentation/profile, current update, exhibit, task, option labels and explanation. Key position and author difficulty/acceptance claims were not evidence. The one kept legacy record, 11 proposed legacy retirements and separate unscored functioning-nerve invasion hold were noted but not independently adjudicated. No held or parked node was treated as executable.

Review-wide limitations: this is an offline editorial review, not independent source verification or clinical approval. All versions remain needs_clinician_review. Difficulty and highYield are qualitative educational judgments, not measured exam frequencies. Runtime rendering, answer randomization and wait estimates cannot be certified from the permitted visible fields; no fixed waits occur in this candidate prose. Each case supplies one consistent age/sex profile and a short complaint. All proposed exhibits are null.

No reliable wording-only shortcut uniquely separates CT from PET-CT; the concern is shallow clinical discrimination, not fabricated lexical cueing. Adult neck-mass evaluation is a high-yield objective.
suggestions: Retain the persistent lesion and actual acoustic limitation. Rebuild the decision around interpretation of a genuinely competing prior study or acquisition issue so a repeat examination remains initially reasonable and a specific observation changes the next study.
Replace the systemic-staging foil with a credible competing local workup strategy supported by the revised case. Do not merely add MRI and declare it inferior without a patient-specific reason.
If this remains a straightforward foundational imaging item, seek explicit acceptance of that role instead of describing it as difficult two-step resident reasoning.

review.title: R02 — Initial acquisition from a partly cystic neck mass

cues.phrase: Which initial tissue procedure / Ultrasound-guided FNA of the tissue component
cues.why: The task's tissue wording is repeated only in the key's target label. This is a weak lexical nudge, not proof that fluid sampling is never diagnostic; it reinforces an already elementary target contrast.

fairness: Image-guided FNA directed at viable enhancing tissue is the best offered initial acquisition. FNA of the fluid component is less representative; an initial open excision is a credible classic error but substantially less attractive at this stage. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Technique and target are nominally two choices, but one option is the familiar premature open-biopsy error and the remaining pair directly contrasts tissue with fluid. The actual discrimination is easy rather than two substantial reasoning steps.

The CT update coherently follows R01 and supplies accessible cervical tissue and lack of continuity with a major vessel. R01 feedback does not preteach this answer. With the shared presentation and this update, the question stands independently of answering R01 correctly.
The explanatory caveat about core sampling appropriately avoids a universal FNA-over-core claim. Adult cystic neck-mass sampling is high yield.
suggestions: Use a neutral complete lead-in such as which sampling procedure to request for the imaged cervical mass, avoiding key-only repetition of tissue.

Make technique and target selection depend on a clinically meaningful acquisition or adequacy finding and compare credible sampling plans at that same stage. Do not add core as a distractor without information that distinguishes it.
Retain the observed solid/fluid anatomy and vascular relationship; hiding those facts would impair fairness rather than improve difficulty.

review.title: R03 — Tissue architecture after unresolved lymphoid sampling
clarityIssues: The explanation's sentence about a new surgical-architecture objective and an old core-after-FNA rule refers to authoring history that a resident has not been given. It does not explain the clinical choice.

cues.phrase: Repeat core biopsy of a cervical node / Repeat FNA biopsy of a cervical node
cues.why: Both distractors explicitly repeat the two procedures that the presentation has just described as insufficient. The key is the only new acquisition, allowing a try-something-different strategy without understanding lymphoid architecture.

cues.phrase: He takes no anticoagulant and has no previous neck operation.
cues.why: Together with the superficial mobile node and vessel separation, these extra surgical-permission details point toward the sole operative option. The actual anatomy is relevant, but the cumulative scaffolding makes the intended escalation conspicuous.

fairness: Excisional biopsy is a defensible best answer for a suspected T-cell lymphoid process that remains unclassified after viable cores lacking preserved organization, when an accessible node is described. I do not identify a confident clinical error in the key.
The nodal-organization finding is decision-critical and should remain. It is legitimate pathology evidence, not an error merely because it supports excision.

The item mainly tests recognition that larger tissue architecture is needed after inadequate classification. The two already-unsuccessful repeat procedures do not sustain a second consequential decision. Lymphoma tissue architecture is high yield; exact subtype-specific acquisition claims still require clinician review.

This is a standalone node, with no sequence dependency. The ultrasound attribution of a mobile node is awkward: mobility is ordinarily a clinical examination observation, whereas the vessel relationship is an ultrasound finding.
suggestions: Replace authoring-history commentary with a short explanation of why viable cells can still fail to establish nodal architecture and why the offered repeat methods are less useful here.
Attribute mobility to examination and separation from vessels to ultrasound.

If retaining resident-level difficulty, make specimen adequacy or target selection genuinely distinguish a plausible repeat acquisition from excision; avoid making both distractors unqualified repeats of documented failures.
Trim nonessential procedural-permission details while preserving actual surgical accessibility and any real contraindication needed to rank the options.

review.title: N01 — Intervention after failed basket capture of a distal duct stone
fairness: Transoral incision and extraction is the defensible best offered intervention for a fixed distal submandibular duct stone reached but not captured endoscopically. The case does not imply that failed basket capture requires gland excision.

The two consequential steps are interpreting the failed procedure as a capture/impaction problem rather than failure to reach the stone, then using distal localization to select extraction over fragmentation or gland removal. These facts materially determine the action.

All three choices are specific procedures of comparable form. The anatomical words are necessary data, not a unique wording match to the key. No strong length, convergence, absolute or pre-answer teaching cue identified.

The clinical diagnosis is properly supplied for a treatment decision. Absence of fever or purulent drainage supports the nonacute treatment stage. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; comparisons with unoffered techniques are not needed to establish the best offered choice.

N01's explanation does not reveal N02's subsequent residual-stone management. The later stone-removal update follows coherently. Location-dependent management of symptomatic salivary stones is high yield.
suggestions: Preserve the exact distinction between reaching the stone and failing to pass a basket around it; do not simplify this to nonspecific failed sialendoscopy.
Keep this editorial PASS separate from Melissa Rowland's exact-version clinical approval.

review.title: N02 — Asymptomatic residual intraparenchymal calcification
clarityIssues: The residual focus was not described in the initial presentation. The term still implies an earlier documented intraparenchymal focus, although the preceding record described only the distal duct stone. A resident can infer a second focus, but the chronology should state it directly.
fairness: Clinical follow-up is a defensible best answer for the asymptomatic residual intraparenchymal finding with restored clear salivary flow. The explanation says conservative follow-up can be appropriate and does not claim that all retained stones should always be ignored.

The symptom resolution is essential clinical evidence, not an unfair clue that should be removed. However, the offered alternatives are another extraction beyond the previously entered segment and removal of the now-functioning gland. This makes observation a straightforward choice with little remaining conflict.

The update is necessary and does change management from N01, but its interpretation and application amount to the single simple rule of not intervening merely to clear an asymptomatic image. The intraparenchymal detail mainly makes the procedural alternatives still less attractive.

The treatment response follows N01 coherently, and N01's explanation does not state this answer. Apart from the still chronology issue, the shared presentation plus update supports independent answering.

General symptom-driven salivary management is useful, but this exact residual intraparenchymal-stone surveillance distinction is lower-yield than initial neck-mass workup, symptomatic stone treatment or malignant facial-nerve findings. This is a qualitative prioritization, not a claim about measured exam frequency.
suggestions: Say follow-up ultrasound shows an additional intraparenchymal focus, or document that focus in the preceding record, without implying that the removed distal stone persists.
Consider merging this into N01's post-answer teaching instead of using another scored node for the uncomplicated recovery state.

review.title: N01 — Intervention after failed basket capture of a distal duct stone
fairness: Transoral incision and extraction is the defensible best offered intervention for a fixed distal submandibular duct stone reached but not captured endoscopically. The case does not imply that failed basket capture requires gland excision.

The two consequential steps are interpreting the failed procedure as a capture/impaction problem rather than failure to reach the stone, then using distal localization to select extraction over fragmentation or gland removal. These facts materially determine the action.

All three choices are specific procedures of comparable form. The anatomical words are necessary data, not a unique wording match to the key. No strong length, convergence, absolute or pre-answer teaching cue identified.

The clinical diagnosis is properly supplied for a treatment decision. Absence of fever or purulent drainage supports the nonacute treatment stage. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; comparisons with unoffered techniques are not needed to establish the best offered choice.

N01's explanation does not reveal N02's subsequent residual-stone management. The later stone-removal update follows coherently. Location-dependent management of symptomatic salivary stones is high yield.
suggestions: Preserve the exact distinction between reaching the stone and failing to pass a basket around it; do not simplify this to nonspecific failed sialendoscopy.
Keep this editorial PASS separate from Melissa Rowland's exact-version clinical approval.

review.title: N06 — Microscopic perineural invasion after complete low-grade tumor excision
fairness: Postoperative regional radiotherapy is the defensible best offered plan for multidisciplinary discussion when microscopic perineural invasion is found despite clear margins. Surveillance is a credible near-miss because the tumor is small, low grade and node negative. Routine cisplatin intensification is not established merely by this finding.

The learner must identify perineural invasion from tumor within small nerve sheaths, then apply that adverse feature despite otherwise favorable pathology. The update materially changes the surveillance-versus-adjuvant-treatment decision. These are two consequential steps.

The diagnosis label is withheld appropriately while the actual pathological observation is supplied. No unique wording echo, answer-length outlier, rhetorical absolute or pre-answer explanation identifies radiotherapy. The two radiotherapy-containing options still require deciding whether systemic intensification is warranted.

The small nerves are explicitly separate from the main facial nerve. This preserves coherence with N05 and makes the later question interpretable using the shared presentation and update. N05's explanation does not teach postoperative irradiation.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The recommendation is for team discussion, not a specified regimen or claim of guaranteed benefit. Exact histotype-specific evidence and final treatment planning remain for clinician review. Perineural invasion as an adverse postoperative feature is high yield.
suggestions: Preserve both the favorable pathology and the anatomically distinct microscopic nerve finding; those details create the useful competition with surveillance.
Keep the explanation's distinction between gross facial-nerve involvement and microscopic small-nerve invasion, and do not add an unsupported radiotherapy regimen or mandatory cisplatin rule.
Keep this editorial PASS separate from Melissa Rowland's exact-version clinical approval.

beforeNodes.task: Which imaging study should be requested next to assess {patientName}'s neck mass?

choices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck
choices.rationale: Cross-sectional contrast imaging assesses the deep extent not shown by ultrasound.
choices.temptation: Recognize an unresolved anatomy question.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: A resolving superficial node already completely mapped would not need this escalation.

choices.label: Repeat ultrasound of the neck
choices.rationale: Repeating the superficial window may leave the retroclavicular extent unresolved.
choices.temptation: Ultrasound is useful for accessible cervical targets.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: An accessible target with an inadequate first acquisition could warrant repeat ultrasound.

choices.label: FDG PET-CT of the body
choices.rationale: Metabolic staging does not replace the dedicated local anatomical assessment needed here.
choices.temptation: Persistent adenopathy raises concern for systemic malignancy.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: A tissue-proven malignancy needing disease-specific systemic staging could warrant PET-CT.

beforeNodes.explanation: Persistent unexplained adenopathy warrants evaluation. Dedicated contrast CT is the best offered study for the incompletely visualized deep extent; MRI could be appropriate in another offered set.
steps: Recognize that resolved throat symptoms have not explained the persistent solid lesion.
Use the missing deep boundary to choose dedicated cross-sectional assessment.
beforeNodes.closestError: Repeat a surface study because it already found the lump.
beforeNodes.decider: The lower lesion margin extends beyond the ultrasound window behind the clavicle.
beforeNodes.consequence: Delayed evaluation from accepting incomplete local characterization.
beforeNodes.counterfactual: If the mass resolved and a complete scan showed normal nodes, this further assessment would not follow.

beforeNodes.task: Which initial tissue procedure should {patientName}'s team request for the imaged neck mass?

choices.label: Ultrasound-guided FNA of the tissue component
choices.rationale: Targeted FNA samples the represented tissue rather than treating cyst contents as the whole lesion.
choices.temptation: Combine the initial needle method with a representative target.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: An accessible collection requiring fluid analysis for an infectious question has a different target.

choices.label: Ultrasound-guided FNA of the fluid component
choices.rationale: Cyst contents may not represent the underlying lesional tissue.
choices.temptation: The fluid center is a large visible target and aspiration may collapse the lump.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Fluid aspiration is appropriate when the diagnostic question concerns a suspected infected collection or when separately planned cyst-fluid analysis is required.

choices.label: Open excisional biopsy of the entire neck mass
choices.rationale: An unplanned open diagnostic operation should not replace the initial representative needle approach.
choices.temptation: Removing all of an adult cystic mass can seem more definitive than sampling it.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Unresolved suitable needle workup, or a separate architectural requirement, can warrant planned surgical biopsy.

beforeNodes.currentUpdate: The contrast CT shows the mass at the left jugular nodal chain, with a fluid-containing center and an enhancing tissue portion along its wall. A cervical portion lies beneath the skin, with extension behind the clavicle. The thyroid and salivary glands are separate; the lesion has no continuity with a major vessel.
beforeNodes.explanation: Use both technique and target: the best offered initial acquisition is image-guided FNA directed at the tissue component. Fluid contents may not represent the lesion. Selected core sampling can also be appropriate, and is not ranked below FNA in this set.
steps: Interpret the fluid-containing nodal mass as an unresolved adult neck lesion with a separate tissue target.
Select representative initial needle sampling rather than cyst-fluid sampling or an unplanned open operation.
beforeNodes.closestError: Choose the easiest fluid target and mistake collapse of the lump for representative tissue acquisition.
beforeNodes.decider: The wall contains enhancing tissue separate from the fluid center, and no needle tissue has yet been obtained.
beforeNodes.consequence: An avoidable open neck biopsy before planned diagnosis.
beforeNodes.counterfactual: If the target were an infected fluid collection requiring culture rather than an unexplained tissue-containing cervical mass, fluid aspiration would become appropriate.

beforeNodes.task: Which biopsy should be requested next to classify {patientName}'s cervical lymphoid process?

choices.label: Excisional biopsy of a cervical node
choices.rationale: Surgical tissue preserves architecture for the unresolved suspected T-cell process.
choices.temptation: Distinguish abnormal cells from an adequate diagnosis.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Disproportionately risky surgical access can favor planned core acquisition.

choices.label: Repeat core biopsy of a cervical node
choices.rationale: Core may suit patients who cannot undergo surgery but does not outrank this represented superficial surgical target after unresolved cores.
choices.temptation: Core obtained viable cells and avoids an operation.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: A high-risk deep surgical target with a feasible needle route may favor cores.

choices.label: Repeat FNA biopsy of a cervical node
choices.rationale: Aspirated cells do not restore the absent nodal architecture.
choices.temptation: More flow material might appear sufficient after an abnormal result.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Optimized FNA can resolve a cytology-suitable epithelial question after an acellular or mistargeted sample.

beforeNodes.explanation: An aberrant population does not complete classification. The suspected T-cell process remains unresolved after cores, and the superficial node supports surgical tissue acquisition. This new surgical-architecture objective does not promote the old core-after-FNA rule.
steps: Separate abnormal-cell detection from architectural diagnosis.
Use the unresolved T-cell differential and represented superficial access to choose surgical tissue.
beforeNodes.closestError: Treat abnormal flow or viable cores as a completed lymphoma classification.
beforeNodes.decider: Viable but disorganized cores cannot classify the process, while a superficial node separated from major vessels is represented.
beforeNodes.consequence: Persistent nondiagnosis and delayed entity-specific treatment.
beforeNodes.counterfactual: If only a deep high-risk surgical target existed, with a feasible percutaneous route, planned core acquisition could become appropriate.
beforeNodes.attack: Removed third identical, least invasive and the unsupported inference that vessel proximity makes core safer. All options acquire tissue. Actual superficial anatomy is necessary evidence for the excision/core boundary, not a promise of service availability.

beforeNodes.objective: Choose intervention for a fixed accessible duct stone
beforeNodes.task: Which intervention should be recommended next for {patientName}'s submandibular duct stone?

choices.label: Transoral duct incision and stone extraction
choices.rationale: The reachable fixed distal stone allows a duct approach that preserves the gland.
choices.temptation: Use actual site and retrieval limitations rather than jump to gland removal.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: An inaccessible intraparenchymal stone would require a different plan.

choices.label: Extracorporeal shock-wave stone fragmentation
choices.rationale: This serves selected stones not directly accessible through a duct approach.
choices.temptation: A failed basket can make lithotripsy seem the automatic next step.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: A symptomatic poorly accessible intraparenchymal stone may justify specialist lithotripsy.

choices.label: Transcervical submandibular gland excision
choices.rationale: Gland removal is disproportionate before addressing this accessible duct stone.
choices.temptation: Recurrent symptoms may be mistaken for irreversible gland failure.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Persistent symptomatic disease after suitable alternatives can warrant gland excision.

beforeNodes.explanation: Use location and actual access to choose the intervention. Failed basket capture of a fixed distal stone can lead to transoral extraction rather than removal of the whole gland.
steps: Connect meal-linked swelling and the located duct stone to mechanical outflow obstruction.
Use distal access and failed basket capture to choose a different gland-preserving route.
beforeNodes.closestError: Treat failed basket capture as failure of every gland-preserving method.
beforeNodes.decider: A fixed distal stone is palpable and was reached; the basket could not surround it.
beforeNodes.consequence: Avoidable loss of the gland and operative morbidity.
beforeNodes.counterfactual: Move the symptomatic stone to a nonpalpable inaccessible intraparenchymal branch and direct duct incision loses its basis.
beforeNodes.attack: Three real salivary interventions. Removed a gland-preserving lead-in. A failed basket is an observed limitation, not endoscopy unavailability. No source size cutoff, success rate or universal procedure ladder is invented.
beforeNodes.category: Three definitive salivary procedures at the intervention stage.
beforeNodes.deletion: Both location and retrieval record earn their place. Location without the basket limitation permits several extraction techniques; failed basket capture without location does not identify a transoral route. Feedback does not discuss residual asymptomatic stones.
beforeNodes.difficultyReason: The credible error overgeneralizes an access failure into the need for gland resection.

beforeNodes.objective: Choose follow-up for a residual intraparenchymal stone
beforeNodes.task: Which follow-up plan best fits {patientName}'s residual salivary finding?

choices.label: Clinical follow-up for recurrent gland symptoms
choices.rationale: A residual image finding without current symptoms does not itself justify another procedure.
choices.temptation: Distinguish visible stone from persistent symptomatic obstruction.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Recurrent pain, swelling or infection triggers reassessment.

choices.label: Repeat sialendoscopy for residual stone extraction
choices.rationale: Another extraction has no demonstrated symptomatic target here.
choices.temptation: A visible remnant may be mistaken for failed treatment.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: An accessible residual stone causing recurrent obstruction could warrant repeat endoscopy.

choices.label: Elective referral for submandibular gland excision
choices.rationale: Gland removal to clear an asymptomatic image is not supported by this record.
choices.temptation: An inaccessible residual focus can seem to demand definitive clearance.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: Persistent symptomatic intraparenchymal disease after suitable alternatives may favor gland excision.

beforeNodes.currentUpdate: After transoral stone removal, meal-related swelling and pain stop and clear saliva flows from the duct. Follow-up ultrasound still shows a small calcific focus within an intraparenchymal branch beyond the segment entered at sialendoscopy.
beforeNodes.explanation: Read the residual image alongside current function. Conservative follow-up can be appropriate for an asymptomatic intraparenchymal stone; gland removal is not required to make the image stone-free.
steps: Separate restored function from the residual imaging focus.
Choose symptom-based follow-up rather than intervention solely to normalize imaging.
beforeNodes.closestError: Use stone-free imaging as the required endpoint of successful treatment.
beforeNodes.decider: Meal-related symptoms stopped and saliva flows; the remaining focus is intraparenchymal.
beforeNodes.consequence: Unnecessary repeat intervention despite functional recovery.
beforeNodes.counterfactual: Recurrent meal-related swelling with obstructed flow at the residual branch would replace simple follow-up with reassessment for intervention.

beforeNodes.task: Which sampling procedure should {patientName}'s team request next for the parotid mass?

choices.label: Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy
choices.rationale: Core tissue can supply histological relationships unavailable in the viable unresolved cytology.
choices.temptation: Recognize a material-type limitation rather than assume no cells were collected.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: An acellular fluid-center sample could support better-targeted repeat aspiration.

choices.label: Ultrasound-guided repeat FNA biopsy
choices.rationale: Another cell preparation may remain unable to distinguish these histotypes.
choices.temptation: Repeat FNA can correct inadequate yield or preparation.
choices.correctUnderCounterfactual: An initially acellular or poorly prepared aspirate may be clarified by targeted FNA and adequacy assessment.

choices.label: Open incisional parotid biopsy

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: Which imaging study should be requested next to assess {patientName}'s neck mass?

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck
answerChoices.rationale: Cross-sectional contrast imaging assesses the deep extent not shown by ultrasound.

answerChoices.label: Repeat ultrasound of the neck
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the superficial window may leave the retroclavicular extent unresolved.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating the superficial window may leave the retroclavicular extent unresolved.

answerChoices.label: FDG PET-CT of the body
answerChoices.rationale: Metabolic staging does not replace the dedicated local anatomical assessment needed here.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Metabolic staging does not replace the dedicated local anatomical assessment needed here.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: Persistent unexplained adenopathy warrants evaluation. Dedicated contrast CT is the best offered study for the incompletely visualized deep extent; MRI could be appropriate in another offered set.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: Which initial tissue procedure should {patientName}'s team request for the imaged neck mass?

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided FNA of the tissue component
answerChoices.rationale: Targeted FNA samples the represented tissue rather than treating cyst contents as the whole lesion.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided FNA of the fluid component
answerChoices.rationale: Cyst contents may not represent the underlying lesional tissue.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Cyst contents may not represent the underlying lesional tissue.

answerChoices.label: Open excisional biopsy of the entire neck mass
answerChoices.rationale: An unplanned open diagnostic operation should not replace the initial representative needle approach.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An unplanned open diagnostic operation should not replace the initial representative needle approach.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: Use both technique and target: the best offered initial acquisition is image-guided FNA directed at the tissue component. Fluid contents may not represent the lesion. Selected core sampling can also be appropriate, and is not ranked below FNA in this set.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: Which biopsy should be requested next to classify {patientName}'s cervical lymphoid process?

answerChoices.label: Excisional biopsy of a cervical node
answerChoices.rationale: Surgical tissue preserves architecture for the unresolved suspected T-cell process.

answerChoices.label: Repeat core biopsy of a cervical node
answerChoices.rationale: Core may suit patients who cannot undergo surgery but does not outrank this represented superficial surgical target after unresolved cores.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Core may suit patients who cannot undergo surgery but does not outrank this represented superficial surgical target after unresolved cores.

answerChoices.label: Repeat FNA biopsy of a cervical node
answerChoices.rationale: Aspirated cells do not restore the absent nodal architecture.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Aspirated cells do not restore the absent nodal architecture.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: An aberrant population does not complete classification. The suspected T-cell process remains unresolved after cores, and the superficial node supports surgical tissue acquisition. This new surgical-architecture objective does not promote the old core-after-FNA rule.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: Which intervention should be recommended next for {patientName}'s submandibular duct stone?

answerChoices.label: Transoral duct incision and stone extraction
answerChoices.rationale: The reachable fixed distal stone allows a duct approach that preserves the gland.

answerChoices.label: Extracorporeal shock-wave stone fragmentation
answerChoices.rationale: This serves selected stones not directly accessible through a duct approach.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This serves selected stones not directly accessible through a duct approach.

answerChoices.label: Transcervical submandibular gland excision
answerChoices.rationale: Gland removal is disproportionate before addressing this accessible duct stone.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Gland removal is disproportionate before addressing this accessible duct stone.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: Use location and actual access to choose the intervention. Failed basket capture of a fixed distal stone can lead to transoral extraction rather than removal of the whole gland.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: Which follow-up plan best fits {patientName}'s residual salivary finding?

answerChoices.label: Clinical follow-up for recurrent gland symptoms
answerChoices.rationale: A residual image finding without current symptoms does not itself justify another procedure.

answerChoices.label: Repeat sialendoscopy for residual stone extraction
answerChoices.rationale: Another extraction has no demonstrated symptomatic target here.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Another extraction has no demonstrated symptomatic target here.

answerChoices.label: Elective referral for submandibular gland excision
answerChoices.rationale: Gland removal to clear an asymptomatic image is not supported by this record.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Gland removal to clear an asymptomatic image is not supported by this record.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: Read the residual image alongside current function. Conservative follow-up can be appropriate for an asymptomatic intraparenchymal stone; gland removal is not required to make the image stone-free.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: Which sampling procedure should {patientName}'s team request next for the parotid mass?

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: Core tissue can supply histological relationships unavailable in the viable unresolved cytology.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided repeat FNA biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: Another cell preparation may remain unable to distinguish these histotypes.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Another cell preparation may remain unable to distinguish these histotypes.

answerChoices.label: Open incisional parotid biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: Opening the intact major gland is generally avoided before suitable needle tissue assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Opening the intact major gland is generally avoided before suitable needle tissue assessment.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: The FNA obtained viable lesional cells but did not resolve histotype. A selected core is a supported next acquisition; no fixed number of failed aspirations or universal need for core is asserted.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: Which imaging request best completes local assessment of {patientName}'s parotid cancer?

answerChoices.label: Contrast MRI of the neck and skull base
answerChoices.rationale: MRI supplies preferred local soft-tissue assessment for this malignancy and new nerve findings.

answerChoices.label: Bone-focused CT of the skull base
answerChoices.rationale: Bone-focused CT does not supply the same soft-tissue assessment for the new neurological concern.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Bone-focused CT does not supply the same soft-tissue assessment for the new neurological concern.

answerChoices.label: FDG PET-CT of the body
answerChoices.rationale: Systemic staging cannot replace the specific local question raised by examination.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Systemic staging cannot replace the specific local question raised by examination.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: The new weakness and sensory change alter the local extent question. Contrast MRI is the best offered local study; dedicated bone assessment and distant staging answer different questions.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: During {patientName}'s recorded parotid cancer operation, which facial-nerve plan was appropriate at the described stage?

answerChoices.label: Preserve the exposed facial nerve branches
answerChoices.rationale: Normal function and separation support preservation during adequate tumor resection.

answerChoices.label: Resect the adjacent branches and graft them
answerChoices.rationale: Proximity does not establish the invasion needed to sacrifice functioning branches.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Proximity does not establish the invasion needed to sacrifice functioning branches.

answerChoices.label: Resect the main nerve trunk and graft it
answerChoices.rationale: The uninvolved functioning trunk has no demonstrated reason for sacrifice.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The uninvolved functioning trunk has no demonstrated reason for sacrifice.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: Parotid malignancy does not itself require nerve sacrifice. Preserve the functioning separable branches while completing tumor resection. Gross invasion of a functioning nerve is a separate withheld boundary.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: Which postoperative plan should {patientName}'s clinic recommend for discussion with the head-and-neck team?

answerChoices.label: Postoperative radiotherapy to the operative region
answerChoices.rationale: Tumor growth inside small nerve sheaths is an adverse feature despite clear margins.

answerChoices.label: MRI surveillance of the operative region
answerChoices.rationale: Size, grade and margin status do not negate the new perineural adverse feature.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Size, grade and margin status do not negate the new perineural adverse feature.

answerChoices.label: Postoperative cisplatin with regional radiotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Routine chemotherapy addition has no established benefit in this setting.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Routine chemotherapy addition has no established benefit in this setting.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: Tumor within small nerve sheaths is perineural growth. It supports postoperative local radiotherapy discussion despite clear resection; it does not prove that the spared main facial nerve should have been removed. Routine cisplatin addition is unsupported.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: During {patientName}'s outside admission for worsening parotid swelling, which imaging request was appropriate next?

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck
answerChoices.rationale: CT can assess a deep collection and extent hidden from ultrasound.

answerChoices.label: Repeat surface ultrasound of the parotid
answerChoices.rationale: The surface window may still leave the mandible-obscured deep compartment unseen.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The surface window may still leave the mandible-obscured deep compartment unseen.

answerChoices.label: Noncontrast CT of the neck
answerChoices.rationale: Unenhanced CT can show calcification but lacks the enhancement information needed to map complicated soft-tissue infection.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Unenhanced CT can show calcification but lacks the enhancement information needed to map complicated soft-tissue infection.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: The prior examination did not visualize the deep gland, and the recorded course worsened. Contrast CT assesses a possible deep collection and extent. Airway deterioration would demand urgent assessment before routine imaging.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: Which imaging request was appropriate after cervical drainage in {patientName}'s outside deep-neck infection admission?

answerChoices.label: Contrast CT of the neck and chest
answerChoices.rationale: The new thoracic finding requires mapping the cervical source and possible inferior extension.

answerChoices.label: Contrast CT limited to the neck
answerChoices.rationale: A neck-only field can miss the inferior focus suggested by retrosternal pain.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A neck-only field can miss the inferior focus suggested by retrosternal pain.

answerChoices.label: CT pulmonary angiography of the chest
answerChoices.rationale: A pulmonary-arterial protocol does not evaluate the entire neck-to-thorax infection pathway.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A pulmonary-arterial protocol does not evaluate the entire neck-to-thorax infection pathway.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: Persistent fever and new retrosternal pain after deep neck infection raise concern for inferior extension even as the neck improves. Contrast neck-and-chest imaging maps the connected compartments.

beforeCompiledQuestions.stem: Which additional source-control plan should {patientName}'s hospital team arrange after this CT?

answerChoices.label: Thoracic surgical drainage of the mediastinal collection
answerChoices.rationale: The persistent infected collection lies in the mediastinum and needs additional drainage planning.

answerChoices.label: Pleural catheter drainage of the right hemithorax
answerChoices.rationale: Pleural drainage does not enter the represented mediastinal collection.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Pleural drainage does not enter the represented mediastinal collection.

answerChoices.label: Repeat drainage of the original cervical cavity
answerChoices.rationale: The original cavity is collapsed while the inferior collection persists.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The original cavity is collapsed while the inferior collection persists.

beforeCompiledQuestions.explanation: The new collection is separate from the collapsed cervical cavity and from the pleura. Arrange multidisciplinary mediastinal source control while antibiotics continue. The exact access route depends on full extent and specialist assessment.

beforeCompiledNodes.stem: During {patientName}'s recorded parotid cancer operation, which facial-nerve plan was appropriate at the described stage?

answerChoices.label: Preserve the exposed facial nerve branches
answerChoices.rationale: Normal function and separation support preservation during adequate tumor resection.

answerChoices.label: Resect the adjacent branches and graft them
answerChoices.rationale: Proximity does not establish the invasion needed to sacrifice functioning branches.

answerChoices.label: Resect the main nerve trunk and graft it
answerChoices.rationale: The uninvolved functioning trunk has no demonstrated reason for sacrifice.

beforeCompiledNodes.explanation: Parotid malignancy does not itself require nerve sacrifice. Preserve the functioning separable branches while completing tumor resection. Gross invasion of a functioning nerve is a separate withheld boundary.
sourceLabels: Jarrod J Homer et al. (2024): Head and Neck Cancer: United Kingdom National Multidisciplinary Guidelines, Sixth Edition

beforeCompiledNodes.currentUpdate: Final pathology shows the small low-grade tumor completely excised with uninvolved inked margins. In sections away from the main facial nerve, tumor nests are present inside the sheaths of small nerves. Regional nodes are negative.
beforeCompiledNodes.stem: Which postoperative plan should {patientName}'s clinic recommend for discussion with the head-and-neck team?

answerChoices.label: Postoperative radiotherapy to the operative region
answerChoices.rationale: Tumor growth inside small nerve sheaths is an adverse feature despite clear margins.

answerChoices.label: MRI surveillance of the operative region
answerChoices.rationale: Size, grade and margin status do not negate the new perineural adverse feature.

answerChoices.label: Postoperative cisplatin with regional radiotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Routine chemotherapy addition has no established benefit in this setting.

beforeCompiledNodes.explanation: Tumor within small nerve sheaths is perineural growth. It supports postoperative local radiotherapy discussion despite clear resection; it does not prove that the spared main facial nerve should have been removed. Routine cisplatin addition is unsupported.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck
answerChoices.rationale: CT can assess a deep collection and extent hidden from ultrasound.

answerChoices.label: Repeat surface ultrasound of the parotid

answerChoices.rationale: Unenhanced CT can show calcification but lacks the enhancement information needed to map complicated soft-tissue infection.

beforeCompiledNodes.explanation: The prior examination did not visualize the deep gland, and the recorded course worsened. Contrast CT assesses a possible deep collection and extent. Airway deterioration would demand urgent assessment before routine imaging.

beforeCompiledNodes.stem: Which imaging request was appropriate after cervical drainage in {patientName}'s outside deep-neck infection admission?

answerChoices.label: Contrast CT of the neck and chest
answerChoices.rationale: The new thoracic finding requires mapping the cervical source and possible inferior extension.

answerChoices.label: Contrast CT limited to the neck
answerChoices.rationale: A neck-only field can miss the inferior focus suggested by retrosternal pain.

answerChoices.label: CT pulmonary angiography of the chest
answerChoices.rationale: A pulmonary-arterial protocol does not evaluate the entire neck-to-thorax infection pathway.

beforeCompiledNodes.explanation: Persistent fever and new retrosternal pain after deep neck infection raise concern for inferior extension even as the neck improves. Contrast neck-and-chest imaging maps the connected compartments.
